d: Unknown, unknowable.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “unknown”—something not known, recognized, or identified. It describes a lack of knowledge rather than naming a specific person, object, or event. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 17:23, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its central idea remains clear: what is unknown has not been known or identified by those considering it.

d: Amphipolis, a leading city of Macedonia.

e.t: This word is the name Amphipolis, a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. As a name, it identifies a specific location rather than expressing a general concept or instruction. It occurs once, in Acts 17:1, and English translations retain the name as “Amphipolis.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To unveil, uncover.
me: Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Dative, Singular, Neuter
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “to unveil”: to remove a covering so that something previously hidden becomes visible or known. It describes an act of making something open and revealed rather than concealed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians 3. Its appearance in both an earlier and later verse of that chapter shows its normal focus on something being brought into clear view, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is unveiled.

d: To draw (generally water from a deep well in the ground); perhaps: to draw out.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Plural
Verb, peRfect, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek verb means “to draw,” describing the act of pulling or bringing something toward oneself. In the New Testament, it occurs four times, all in John, and is rendered “draw” in the cited translations. The word functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. Its exact force—what is being drawn and how—comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the movement of something toward the one acting.

d: Apphia, a Christian lady of Colossae, either wife or sister of Philemon.

e.t: Apphia is a personal name, referring to a woman named in the opening greeting of Paul’s letter to Philemon. The word itself functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philemon 1:2, and is rendered as “Apphia.” Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, this entry identifies the person’s name but does not explain her particular role or situation in that passage.

d: A foresail, set on the bow.

e.t: This word means “foresail,” the sail set toward the front of a ship. It is a specific nautical noun rather than a general word for a boat, journey, or sailing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:40, in a passage involving a ship at sea. Since the word names a particular part of the vessel, its meaning is precise: it identifies the forward sail used to help direct or propel the ship. The surrounding verse gives the practical setting in which this maritime term appears.

d: Indestructible, imperishable, incorruptible; hence: immortal.

e.t: This word describes something that cannot decay, perish, or be spoiled: it is “imperishable” and “incorruptible.” In the Greek New Testament, it is used for what endures rather than passing away or being ruined. The word occurs eight times, including descriptions connected with God, resurrection, and an inheritance, though its precise force in each passage comes from the surrounding verse. It is therefore a word of lasting, undiminished quality, contrasting with things subject to corruption or decay.

d: (a) assistance, (b) (a technical term of nautical language), a help.

e.t: This word means “help,” referring to assistance given when support is needed. It is a noun, so it names the aid itself rather than describing the action of helping. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in Acts and Hebrews. Its basic sense remains simple and direct: needed assistance or support. The surrounding passage determines whether that help is practical, as in a situation requiring immediate aid, or associated with approaching God for mercy and grace. The word itself points to help that is available and useful in need.

d: Gallio, Lucius Iunius Gallio, who received this name by adoption into another family, but was born brother of the philosopher Seneca and originally named L. Annaeus Nouatus; proconsul of the Roman province Achaia from spring A.D. 52 to spring 53.

e.t: Gallio is a personal name used to identify a person in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or object. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament, all within Acts 18, in Acts 18:12, 18:14, and 18:17. By itself, the name identifies Gallio; the surrounding verse and passage provide the details about his role and actions.

d: An example, type; a thing shown.

e.t: This word means “example”—something set before others as a demonstration or pattern. It is a noun, naming what serves to illustrate a truth or show the result of a course of action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:7. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the larger context. Its central idea remains clear: a visible example that teaches or warns others.

d: (literal: twain-mouthed; hence: of a sword, as a drinker of blood), two-edged.

e.t: This word means “double-edged,” describing something sharp on both sides. It is an adjective used for an object or image that has two cutting edges rather than only one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Hebrews and Revelation. Its basic sense remains consistent wherever it appears: the thing described has a sharp, cutting quality on both sides. The surrounding verse determines how that image functions in its particular setting.

d: To breathe my last, die, expire.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to die” or “to expire,” describing the end of life. It is a direct word for death rather than a broad description of weakness, sorrow, or danger. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and account, but its central meaning remains the ending of life.

e.t: This word means “six,” the number that comes after five and before seven. It is used in the Greek New Testament as an ordinary number to identify a quantity, time, or count. Its meaning remains direct and precise wherever it appears; the surrounding words determine what is being counted or measured. The word occurs 13 times in 13 New Testament verses, including references in Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, James, and Revelation. It does not itself express a moral quality or spiritual concept; it simply identifies the number six.

d: Of time: when, now, after that; of cause: seeing that, forasmuch as.

e.t: This word means “since” or “when”. It connects one statement with another by indicating the time or circumstance in which something happens. Depending on the sentence, it may introduce what happened “when” something occurred or explain what follows “since” a certain condition exists. It appears 10 times in the Greek New Testament, functioning as a connecting word rather than naming a person, place, object, or action.

d: (a) on the earth, belonging to the earth (as opposed to the sky), (b) in a spiritual sense, belonging to the earthly sphere, earthly (as opposed to heavenly).

e.t: This word means “being on the earth” or “earthly.” It identifies something as belonging to or situated in the earthly realm. The word is used as a description of what is earthly rather than heavenly, but its precise force comes from the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, showing a recurring term for earth-related reality.

d: To fight with wild beasts (i.e. wild beasts in human form); to be exposed to fierce hostility.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This word means “to fight beasts” or “to fight wild animals.” It describes a direct struggle against dangerous animals, rather than a general disagreement or ordinary human conflict. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on battling wild creatures. d: To curse, devote to destruction.

e.t: This word means “to curse”: to speak a curse against someone or pronounce harmful judgment upon them. It describes an action expressed in words, rather than a person, object, or place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its normal meaning is clear, while the exact force of that use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word is found in Matthew 26:74. e.t: This word means “to instruct,” describing the act of teaching or giving someone understanding. It can refer to a person who has been instructed, as well as to the act of instructing others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, showing a recurring idea of receiving or communicating teaching. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on who is teaching, who is being taught, and what is being taught.

d: A small geographical division, district, or territory.

e.t: This word refers to a geographical area or region—a distinct part of a larger land. In the Greek New Testament, it is used three times, and each occurrence is rendered “regions,” supporting the sense of different territories or local areas. It appears in Romans 15:23, 2 Corinthians 11:10, and Galatians 1:21. Its basic meaning is geographical rather than a name for a specific place, so the surrounding verse identifies which region is being discussed.

d: Eloquent, gifted with learning.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “learned,” describing someone recognized for education or knowledge. It points to a person’s intellectual training rather than expressing an action, command, or emotion. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 18:24, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains a description of a person as educated or knowledgeable. [p03:word:greek-nt:G3052:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G3052:occurrences] [p01:word:greek-nt:G3052:reference:0]

d: (a) a scourge, lash, of leathern thongs with pieces of metal sewn up in them, (b) severe pains (sufferings), disease.

e.t: This word means a “flogging device” or “whip,” referring to an instrument used to strike or punish someone. It is a concrete noun rather than a description of pain itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages connected with bodily affliction, punishment, and mistreatment. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the instrument used for flogging. The word appears in Mark, Luke, Acts, and Hebrews.

d: The forehead, front.

e.t: This word means the forehead, the front part of a person’s head above the eyes. It is a noun naming a physical body area, whether referring to one forehead or more than one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, all in Revelation, where the forehead is identified as the location associated with marks or names. The word itself identifies the bodily location; its particular significance in any passage must be understood from that passage’s wording and surrounding context.

d: Adultery.

e.t: This word means adultery: sexual unfaithfulness within marriage. It names the violation of the marital bond rather than merely a general form of wrongdoing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and John. Its use in lists of sinful things and in a narrative involving an accused woman shows that it can refer either to the act itself or to the offense as a recognized category. The exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To form, fashion, shape, mold.
me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “is formed,” “to be formed,” or “to form.” It describes the act or process by which something takes shape or comes into a formed condition. As a verb, it focuses on formation rather than merely naming the finished result. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 4:19, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and sentence. Its basic meaning remains the making or development of something into a recognizable form.

d: Roasted, broiled.

e.t: This word means “broiled,” describing food cooked by direct heat. It is a cooking term rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 24:42. The word’s basic meaning identifies the manner in which food was prepared, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular context in which it appears.

d: To admonish, advise, exhort.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to urge” or “to warn.” It describes addressing someone with earnest counsel or caution, calling for attention to something important. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts 27. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is a serious appeal intended to guide or caution another person.

d: Madness, folly.

e.t: This word means “insanity” or “madness”—a condition of seriously disordered thought or behavior. It describes a loss of sound judgment rather than ordinary confusion or a passing mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:16. The exact force of the word in that verse is best understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to irrational or deranged conduct.

d: A trial, experiment, attempt.

e.t: This word refers to a test or an attempt to do something. It expresses the idea of putting something to the test or trying to carry out an action, depending on how it functions in the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews 11. Its precise sense in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is testing or trying.

e.t: This word means “filled” or “to fill,” describing something becoming full or being supplied with what it needs. It is a verb used across the Greek New Testament, where it may describe a person, place, time, or condition that has reached fullness. The word occurs 24 times in 24 New Testament verses, with especially frequent use in Luke and Acts. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being filled and the surrounding sentence.

d: Rich, abounding in, wealthy; a rich man.

e.t: This word describes someone who is rich—possessing substantial material wealth or abundance. It is an adjective used for people and their circumstances, identifying them as wealthy rather than poor. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, including descriptions of people called rich and references to riches. Its basic sense remains focused on wealth, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about that wealth or the person who has it.

d: Fornication, whoredom; idolatry.

e.t: This word means “sexual immorality” or “sexual sin”—sexual conduct understood as sinful. It is a noun that names this kind of wrongdoing rather than describing a person or action by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 25 times, showing that the term is used across several settings, including Jesus’ teaching, instructions to churches, and Revelation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains sexual behavior identified as sin.

d: Pass: to burn, to be set on fire, to be inflamed; glow with heat, to be purified by fire.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to burn.” It describes the action or condition of burning, whether the surrounding sentence concerns a physical flame, something exposed to fire, or a person experiencing an intense inner feeling. Its precise force depends on what the sentence identifies as burning. The word occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, from 1 Corinthians through Revelation, and is rendered with forms of “burn” in the available translations.

d: A sapphire.

e.t: This word means “sapphire,” referring to a precious blue stone or gem. It is a noun naming the stone itself, rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 21:19. The word’s basic meaning remains the name of the gemstone; the significance it carries in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its description of the setting. This word is the personal name “Saul,” identifying a man rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to Saul in the book of Acts. It occurs nine times across six verses, including passages that record his name being addressed directly and passages that identify him in narrative. The word itself functions as a proper name; its precise significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage.

d: Gloomy, sad-countenanced.

e.t: This word describes someone who is sad or who looks somber. It can refer to an outward appearance that communicates heaviness or unhappiness, rather than naming a particular cause. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 6:16 and Luke 24:17. Its basic sense remains focused on a visibly sad or downcast appearance; the surrounding verse determines why the person looks that way and what the sadness signifies there.

The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of soldiers, warfare, and the conflicts believers must face. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The wording can point to a present act of giving or to what someone will give, depending on the sentence, but its central idea remains grace expressed through giving. It occurs 23 times in the Greek New Testament, across 19 verses, so it is used in more than one setting while retaining this basic sense.

d: O, an exclamation, used in addressing someone.

e.t: This word means “oh!”—a brief exclamation used in speech. It expresses an immediate response and can give emotional force to what follows, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times across 17 verses, showing that it is a recurring speech expression. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its basic sense remains a spoken exclamation.

This word means “gentleness”—a mild, considerate quality expressed in the way a person treats others. It describes strength or conduct that is not harsh, aggressive, or needlessly severe. As a noun, it names this quality rather than describing a particular action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains a calm, gracious manner that avoids roughness and treats others with care.
